ap_physics_1-m01.stem: Climber 1 and climber 2 each have a mass of $70\text{ kg}$ and each climbs at a steady pace up the same vertical rope to a height of $3\text{ m}$. Climber 1 takes $10\text{ s}$ and climber 2 takes $20\text{ s}$. Which statement is correct and best justified?

options.text: Both climbers do the same work of $2060\text{ J}$, but climber 1 has the greater average power of $206\text{ W}$, because power is the work done per unit time.
options.why: Each climber lifts $mg$ through $h$, so $W=mgh=2060\text{ J}$, and $P=W/t$ is $206\text{ W}$ for climber 1 and $103\text{ W}$ for climber 2.

options.text: Both climbers have the same power of $206\text{ W}$, because they do the same work.
options.why: Treats equal work as equal power, forgetting that power is the rate at which the work is done.

options.text: Climber 2 does more work, because climber 2 spends more time exerting a force on the rope.
options.why: Confuses the time spent with the amount of work; the work depends on the force and the distance.

options.text: Climber 2 has the greater power of $103\text{ W}$, because it takes longer to do the work.
options.why: Divides the wrong way or thinks that a longer time means more power, but power decreases as the time increases.

ap_physics_1-m02.stem: An astronaut has a weight of $686\text{ N}$ on the surface of Earth. A planet has $8$ times the mass of Earth and $2$ times the radius of Earth. Which of the following is the best prediction of the weight of the astronaut on the surface of the planet?

options.why: The weight is $GMm/R^2$, which increases by the factor $8$ for the mass and decreases by the factor $2^2=4$ for the radius: $686\text{ N}\times8/4=1370\text{ N}$.
Multiplies the weight by the factor for the mass and the factor for the radius squared.
Multiplies the weight by the factor for the mass only and forgets the radius.
Puts the factor for the radius squared in the numerator and the factor for the mass in the denominator.

(Moments of inertia: hoop $MR^2$, solid disk $\tfrac12MR^2$, solid sphere $\tfrac25MR^2$, thin shell $\tfrac23MR^2$.) Rank the rotational kinetic energies from greatest to least.

options.why: Ranks by the mass times the angular speed squared, ignoring the radius and shape.
Ranks by the moment of inertia alone, ignoring the angular speed.
With $K=\tfrac12I\omega^2$ the rotational kinetic energies in joules are A: 25.9, B: 1.33, C: 0.384, D: 7.20, which ranks as A > D > B > C.
Ranks by the angular speed alone, ignoring the moment of inertia.

ap_physics_1-m09.stem: A $1\text{ kg}$ cart moving at $6\text{ m/s}$ on a frictionless track collides with a stationary $3\text{ kg}$ cart, and the two carts stick together. Which statement about the kinetic energy of the carts is correct and best justified?

options.text: The kinetic energy decreases to $9.00\text{ J}$, because each cart keeps half of the energy.
options.why: Splits the energy equally between the carts without using the masses and the conservation of momentum.

options.text: The kinetic energy increases to $72.0\text{ J}$, because the total mass that moves is greater after the collision.
options.why: Uses the original speed for the combined mass, but the speed decreases after the carts stick together.

options.text: The kinetic energy decreases from $18.0\text{ J}$ to $4.50\text{ J}$, because the carts move together after the collision and the momentum is conserved but the kinetic energy is not.
options.why: $v_f=mv/(m+M)=1.50\text{ m/s}$, so $K_f=\tfrac12(m+M)v_f^2=4.50\text{ J}$, which is less than $18.0\text{ J}$.

options.text: The kinetic energy stays $18.0\text{ J}$, because momentum is conserved in the collision, so the kinetic energy is also conserved.
options.why: Treats conservation of momentum as conservation of kinetic energy, which holds only for elastic collisions.

ap_physics_1-m12.stem: Two skaters stand at rest on frictionless ice. The $60\text{ kg}$ skater pushes the $80\text{ kg}$ skater, and the $60\text{ kg}$ skater moves backward at $1.5\text{ m/s}$. Which statement about the speed of the $80\text{ kg}$ skater is correct and best justified?

options.text: The $80\text{ kg}$ skater moves forward at $1.12\text{ m/s}$, because the total momentum of the two skaters stays zero.
options.why: The skaters form a system with no net horizontal external force, so their momenta are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

options.text: The $80\text{ kg}$ skater moves forward at $1.5\text{ m/s}$, because the push forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
options.why: Takes equal and opposite forces to mean equal speeds, ignoring the different masses.

options.text: The $80\text{ kg}$ skater moves forward at $2\text{ m/s}$, because the speeds are inversely proportional to the masses with the heavier skater faster.
options.why: Inverts the mass ratio so the heavier skater ends up faster.

options.text: The skater who pushed gains all the momentum, because the one who pushes is the one that does the work.
options.why: Thinks that only the pusher gains momentum; the momentum gained by one skater is lost by the other in the total.

ap_physics_1-m12.stem: Two carts at rest on a frictionless track are held together with a compressed spring between them. When the spring is released, the $1\text{ kg}$ cart moves away at $3\text{ m/s}$ to the left. Which statement about the $4\text{ kg}$ cart is correct and best justified?

options.text: It moves to the right at $3\text{ m/s}$, because the spring exerts equal and opposite forces on the two carts.
options.why: Takes equal and opposite forces to mean equal speeds, ignoring that the accelerations depend on the masses.

options.text: It moves to the right at $12\text{ m/s}$, because the lighter cart must have the smaller speed.
options.why: Inverts the mass ratio so the heavier cart ends up faster.

options.text: It stays at rest, because the momentum of each cart is conserved separately.
options.why: Applies conservation of momentum to each cart alone instead of to the system of both carts.

options.text: It moves to the right at $0.75\text{ m/s}$, because the total momentum of the two carts stays zero.
options.why: No net external force acts horizontally, so $0=m_1v_1-m_2v_2$ and the heavier cart moves slower in the opposite direction.
